title: Direct In-Place Database Updates
pattern: A database or storage engine is designed to locate records on disk and overwrite pages at their original file offsets to optimize subsequent point query performance.
why_bad: While locally optimizing point queries (reads can immediately locate and return the record), it severely pessimizes write throughput. In-place updates force the storage engine to perform random writes to different disk blocks. On HDDs, this causes severe mechanical head-positioning delays. On SSDs, it incurs a massive garbage collection penalty because pages must be erased in blocks before they can be rewritten, leading to premature write wear.
detection: Storage designs that perform random-access write operations directly at variable file offsets instead of writing sequentially or buffering in memory.
counterexample: Valid for small configuration files or databases with extremely low write rates. Mark `Context-dependent`.
source: Alex Petrov, *Database Internals*, Chapter 7 "In-place updates vs Append-only" (p. 129) / Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 3 "SSTables and LSM-Trees" (p. 77, 81).
